summary.text: At \(n=5\), direct evaluation gives \(a(4)=3\) and \(a(5)=4\), so the difference is \(1\); however, \(2\phi^2=3+\sqrt5\) has floor \(5\), placing \(5\) in the Beatty set where the difference was claimed to be \(0\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{\sqrt2}+\frac12\right\rfloor,
\]
which is the nearest integer to \(n/\sqrt2\). Also let
\[
\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
The conjecture includes the assertion that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\),
\[
a(n)-a(n-1)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=\lfloor k\phi^2\rfloor\text{ for some integer }k\ge1.
\]
We disprove this assertion at \(n=5\). Since this assertion is one of the conjuncts of the full conjecture, its failure disproves the entire conjecture, independently of the claims involving the zeta tail \(s(m)\).

First we calculate \(a(4)\) and \(a(5)\). We will use the elementary bounds
\[
\frac75<\sqrt2<\frac{71}{50}.
\]
Indeed, all quantities are positive, and
\[
\left(\frac75\right)^2=\frac{49}{25}=1.96<2,
\qquad
\left(\frac{71}{50}\right)^2=\frac{5041}{2500}=2.0164>2.
\]
Taking positive square roots gives the displayed bounds.

For \(n=4\), consider
\[
x_4=\frac4{\sqrt2}+\frac12.
\]
We claim that \(3<x_4<4\). For the lower bound, \(\sqrt2<71/50\), so, because the denominators are positive,
\[
\frac4{\sqrt2}>\frac4{71/50}=\frac{200}{71}>\frac52.
\]
Consequently \(x_4>5/2+1/2=3\). For the upper bound, \(\sqrt2>7/5\), and hence
\[
\frac4{\sqrt2}<\frac4{7/5}=\frac{20}{7}<\frac72.
\]
Thus \(x_4<7/2+1/2=4\). It follows that
\[
a(4)=\lfloor x_4\rfloor=3.
\]

For \(n=5\), put
\[
x_5=\frac5{\sqrt2}+\frac12.
\]
Again using \(\sqrt2<71/50\), we obtain
\[
\frac5{\sqrt2}>\frac5{71/50}=\frac{250}{71}>\frac72,
\]
because \(500>497\). Therefore \(x_5>7/2+1/2=4\). On the other hand, \(\sqrt2>7/5\) gives
\[
\frac5{\sqrt2}<\frac5{7/5}=\frac{25}{7}<\frac92,
\]
so \(x_5<9/2+1/2=5\). Hence
\[
a(5)=\lfloor x_5\rfloor=4.
\]
It follows that the difference at position \(5\) is
\[
a(5)-a(4)=4-3=1,
\]
not \(0\).

It remains to show that \(5\) nevertheless belongs to the claimed zero-position Beatty sequence \(\{\lfloor k\phi^2\rfloor:k\ge1\}\). Take \(k=2\). Since \((\sqrt5)^2=5\),
\[
\phi^2
 =\left(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\right)^2
 =\frac{1+2\sqrt5+5}{4}
 =\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
2\phi^2=3+\sqrt5.
\]
The elementary inequalities
\[
2\le\sqrt5<3
\]
follow by comparing squares: \(4\le5<9\), with all terms nonnegative. Thus
\[
5\le 3+\sqrt5<6,
\]
and consequently
\[
\lfloor2\phi^2\rfloor=\lfloor3+\sqrt5\rfloor=5.
\]
Hence \(5\) is indeed of the form \(\lfloor k\phi^2\rfloor\) with the positive integer \(k=2\).

The conjectured equivalence at \(n=5\) would therefore force
\[
a(5)-a(4)=0,
\]
because \(5=\lfloor2\phi^2\rfloor\). But the direct calculation above gives
\[
a(5)-a(4)=1.
\]
This contradiction disproves the claimed characterization of the zero differences, and therefore disproves the full conjecture.
